site_article.headline: Eric Schmidt says Anthropic beat Google's revenue growth record at more than twice the speed
site_article.dek: The former Google chief executive told a Norwegian podcast that AI is not a bubble, while reports say he holds about 1% of Anthropic.
site_article.summary: Former Google CEO Eric Schmidt said on the In Good Company podcast that Anthropic broke the revenue growth record Google set under his leadership, at more than twice the speed. Bloomberg has reported that Schmidt owns about 1% of Anthropic, a stake that could be worth $15 billion to $20 billion at valuations discussed ahead of its expected IPO.
site_article.seo_title: Eric Schmidt: Anthropic beat Google's growth record, AI no bubble
site_article.seo_description: Former Google CEO Eric Schmidt says Anthropic grew more than twice as fast as Google did and calls AI real growth, not a bubble.
site_article.answer_summary: Eric Schmidt said Anthropic broke Google's revenue growth record at more than twice the speed and argued AI is not a bubble because customers are paying real money. He did not explain how he made the comparison, and Bloomberg reports he owns about 1% of Anthropic.
site_article.hero_alt: Eric Schmidt in a dark suit, photographed at a public event.

paragraphs.text: Eric Schmidt, who led Google as chief executive from 2001 to 2011, said Anthropic has broken the revenue growth record that Google set while he ran the company, and did it at more than twice the speed. He made the remarks on In Good Company, the podcast hosted by Nicolai Tangen, head of Norway's sovereign wealth fund, according to Benzinga, which reported the comments on October 22, 2026.

"When I was CEO at Google, we set the revenue growth record. They smashed it more than twice the speed as we did," Schmidt said, according to Benzinga. Benzinga noted that he did not explain how he calculated the comparison.

Schmidt used the comparison to argue that the current wave of AI spending is not a bubble. "That's real growth there. It's not fake," he said, adding that "it's real money with real customers who are paying for something useful in their eyes." BigGo Finance, which also summarized the interview, reported that he tests whether a technology wave is real by asking whether "the whole ocean is rising."

Recent financial disclosures give some context for the claim. Reuters reported that Anthropic told prospective investors its third quarter revenue rose 45% to $16.8 billion, up from $11.6 billion in the second quarter and $4.7 billion in the first. The company said it was profitable on an adjusted basis, although growth slowed after revenue more than doubled between the first and second quarters, according to the same report as cited by Benzinga.

The picture is not entirely rosy. A draft IPO prospectus reviewed by Reuters showed a net loss of $80.7 billion in the first half of 2026, which included a $72 billion noncash charge tied to convertible financing. Anthropic spent nearly $9 billion on computing and infrastructure over those six months and has committed at least $518 billion over a decade, Benzinga reported.

Schmidt is not a neutral observer. Bloomberg News reported on October 19 that he owns about 1% of Anthropic, according to Reuters. People familiar with the matter said he invested tens of millions of dollars in the company's Series A round. It is unclear whether he has sold any shares, and his representatives declined to comment.

Benzinga said the stake could be worth $15 billion to $20 billion at the valuations discussed ahead of Anthropic's anticipated initial public offering. Reuters has reported that some investors discussed a valuation of around $1.5 trillion, below earlier expectations of roughly $2 trillion.

Schmidt also warned about competition from China. He estimated that Chinese models are about six months behind American ones, according to both write-ups. "If you define losing as users, the vast majority of the world will use the free Chinese models rather than the more expensive Western models," he said, as quoted by Benzinga. BigGo Finance reported that he argued the West is already losing even at a six month lead, because the Chinese strategy is to make the products free.

According to BigGo Finance, Schmidt also said AI agents will push large companies toward cutting roughly 20% of white collar jobs, and argued that European rules written before the technology existed are driving founders and talent to the United States.

Schmidt's comparison is striking, but it comes from an investor who stands to gain from a high Anthropic valuation, and he offered no method behind it. The reported revenue figures support the idea of unusually fast growth, while the large losses and long term computing commitments show why many investors still question whether that growth will last.
The next test is Anthropic's IPO roadshow and final valuation, which will show whether public market investors accept the growth story Schmidt is describing.
